One More Rate Hike Is Looking Like the Beginning, Not the End
 
Plus, a senior U.S. soldier is arrested on allegations of spying for Russia, and a $26 million cyber heist rocks a small New Jersey town
 
 
AL DRAGO/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Good morning. Wall Street’s victory lap on interest rates will have to wait.

 

After weeks of tuning out the Federal Reserve to focus on cracks in the artificial-intelligence trade, investors were jolted yesterday by a one-two punch of hot inflation data and hawkish Fed talk.

 

Core consumer prices rose at a 3.7% annualized rate over the three months through October, leaving little doubt of a December rate increase. The real concern, however, isn’t next month’s move. It’s what follows: A third straight month of firm underlying inflation reopens the question of how far and how fast the central bank must go.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fended off an impeachment effort in the House after GOP votes helped to kill an attempt to punish him for his actions as Pentagon chief.

 

• President Trump’s plan to supply the U.S. with Russian diesel has stalled on the high seas.

 

• A senior U.S. Army soldier assigned to a NATO rapid reaction command structure in the U.K. was arrested on allegations of spying for Russia.

 

• Lawmakers are demanding tighter restrictions on chip exports following Jensen Huang’s affair with a business partner suspected of being a Chinese intelligence source.

 

• Japanese billionaire Masayoshi Son’s huge bet on electrical turbines has backfired.

 

• House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan (R., Ohio) as their leader for the next Congress, embracing new blood after the party’s deep losses in the midterms.

• OpenAI grew revenue by roughly 50% to $10 billion from the second to the third quarter but continued to report heavy operating losses.

 

• One unanswered question in the Nvidia scandal is whether it will pop what many see as an AI investment bubble—a trigger that could ripple through the 401(k)s and pension plans of many Americans, writes Tim Higgins.

 

• CoreWeave’s success hinges on expanding its data center footprint while reducing its cost of capital. Both have become more challenging, writes Asa Fitch.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

An American furniture maker tried to bring jobs back home. It didn’t work.

 

Bruce Krinsky has spent a decade perfecting a sweet spot for sales in the American living room: $900 sofas for shoppers wanting an upgrade over IKEA without splurging on Crate & Barrel. That formula turned TOV Furniture, the company he founded with his wife, into a business pulling in more than $100 million a year. Today, the 44-year-old with a high-school education is living in a Mediterranean-style house in Miami Beach. But for Krinsky, achieving the American dream in the Trump era has been an odyssey. He struggled to stay ahead of changing U.S. policy on trade through a decade in which the nation has wrestled with where it wants its everyday things to be made, reports Stu Woo.

 

5.

 

A $26 million cyber heist is rocking a small New Jersey town.

 

Cranbury, N.J., a historic township of about 4,000 people, is reeling from a distinctly modern catastrophe: a cyber theft to the tune of $26 million after it was tricked into wiring money to the wrong place for a land purchase. At a packed town hall meeting Monday, residents demanded to know how a theft of this scale occurred—and why locals weren’t told of the incident until Friday, three days after a local election. Police confirmed that the municipality would regain $17.3 million, yet that still leaves nearly $9 million unaccounted for. Beyond the financial hit, the crime has shaken public trust in local leaders, reports Scott Calvert.

6. SEE THE STORY

Model Bella Hadid has purchased a house in Crested Butte, Colo., for $5.5 million, according to listing agent Channing Boucher of LIV Sotheby’s International Realty. The roughly 2,000-square-foot house was built in 2001 around two coal-miner sheds dating to the early 1900s. Boucher said the 30-year-old, who appeared in October’s Victoria’s Secret fashion show, has been living in the area for several months; she is dating construction-project manager Nathan Lacy, whose father owns a local construction firm.

8. THE NUMBER

 
$250 million
 

That’s what each of Anthropic’s seven founders plans to cash out in the AI company’s initial public offering—leaving them with stakes worth around $18 billion apiece. The fortunes underscore the sheer scale of Anthropic’s IPO as well as the speed at which the company has grown since its 2021 founding. The company is aiming to go public next week at a valuation of around $1.3 trillion.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Meet the British executive who saves forgotten songs from extinction.

 

By day, London-based Rob Johnson works for a law firm. By night, he’s the Batman of abandoned pop music, wielding his power of impeccable but persistent email etiquette to resuscitate the songs that sit unheard in CD racks around the world. Over the past decade he’s persuaded record labels to upload scores of releases to streaming services, including singles, B-sides, remixes and bonus tracks from the likes of Belinda Carlisle, Sting, Nicole Scherzinger, ’N Sync, Sheryl Crow, the Spice Girls and, in a more obscure success, the Smurfs Greatest Hits.
